Gauteng Health

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With not a single lawsuit decided in the favour of the Gauteng Health Department over the past five years, the Gauteng Health department doesn't seem in a healthy state by the way it is haemorrhaging

Summary:
With not a single lawsuit decided in the favour of the Gauteng Health Department over the past five years, the Gauteng Health department doesn't seem in a healthy state by the way it is haemorrhaging money.
Gauteng Health MEC recently admitted that her department had paid R544 million since 2010 for medical negligence claims. THe department had lost 168 cases and had settled eight out of court.

Further information:
It seems that the department has a policy of wanting to defend every single case against them. If they lose, they apply for leave to appeal, even when leave to appeal by the residing judges are often not granted. Many of the cases makes for harrowing reading and point to negligence of a shocking nature by doctors and nurses who were on duty and treated these patients at the time. Even though these families may win these cases in court and may in the end be compensated in money, their lives are forever changed.

In the legislature in September, the MEC said that the department will not fight unneccesssary court cases and will admit guilt where indicated, but this has not always been the case. Like in the case of our one case study - seven-year old Nonjabulo Mavimbela who was left brain-damaged and now has cerebral palsy after a misdiagnosis of meningitis when she was almost two years old. The department fought fruitlessly for two years to overturn the finding of negligence and her pay-out of R13,1 million.

Chris Hani Baragwanath and Tembisa Hospitals in Gauteng account for the bulk of negligence cases in the province.

According to the department's latest annual report, which was tabled at the Gauteng Legislature in September, legal claims against the department has risen between April 2014 and March 2015 with R4billion, now amounting to R13,1 billion - this comprises of medico-legal claims of R10,1 billion, civil claims of R1,5billion and claims of "premature termination of contracts at R1,5 billion".

It is not likely that the medico-legal claims against the department would all amount into court cases and pay-outs, but it is of concern that there has been such a jump in the number. On average, the department has been paying about R200 million every year for medical negligence in terms of court settlements.

The Gauteng province is not fairing the worst, but it is worrying that the department is defending every single case and also applying for leave to appeal in every single case they have lost - wasting millions of rands in litigations - money that could have been spent otherwise on proper health care development - something the province and the country are lacking.

Our insiders will tell us that in Gauteng's state hospitals patient load is just too big - and maybe that is where some of the negligence in some cases originates from. Some doctors at Baragwanath Hospital have to see between 60 and 80 patients a day - nearly impossible and then to be able to give primal and basic care and attention to every patient is just not likely.

There are regular drug stock-outs in the province's hospitals and in March this year, the Gauteng Health department has been labelled the worst-paying department in the province in terms of its 30-day agreement with suppliers. It seems that the problem has since been rectified, but the Gauteng Health Department is one that is bugged by poor financial management. It hasn't been able to secure a clean audit for many financial years, despite many quick turn-around strategies.

Press Release:


Haemorrhaging Gauteng Health
Seven-year-old Nonjabulo Mavimbela was left brain-damaged and cerebral palsied after a misdiagnosis of TB-meningitis when she was almost two years old. After years of drawn-out litigation she was awarded R13.1- million. Over the past five years, taxpayers have forked out a total of R544-million in damages to compensate many victims of medical negligence like Nonjabulo. With current claims against the Gauteng Health Department at R10-billion, Carte Blanche investigates a health system seemingly failing its patients.


Script:



GAUTENG HEALTH SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

BRENDA MAVIMBELA: When I took Nonjabulo to hospital, she was a normal child, but when we came back home she is brain damaged, and there is no turning back.

Seven-year old Nonjabulo Mavimbela cannot sit by herself, walk, talk or see. She is also brain damaged, has cerebral palsy and epilepsy. Her mother, Brenda and father, Lucky have to care for her 24 hours a day and both had to quit their jobs five years ago in order to do so.
In 2010, Brenda and Lucky’s dreams for their daughter were shattered when she was misdiagnosed at the Far East Rand Hospital, in Johannesburg.

BRENDA: She said mommy its sore here, I said: Let’s take her to the nearest hospital. They said they are going to check if there is the meningitis, they are going to do some fluid on the, a lumbar puncture.

The doctor on duty diagnosed Nonjabulo with Bacterial Meningitis, when in fact she had stage 2 TB Meningitis – which untreated, progressed to stage 3, with a poor prognosis for recovery.
And this misdiagnosis changed Nonjabulo’s life forever.

BRENDA MAVIMBELA: I was crying, I so sad, very sad because he is telling me the way she is not going to be the same as she was before.

Brenda and Lucky sued the department for negligence.
Ruling in their favour and awarding Nonjabulo R13, 1 million, the Judge said that the doctor who treated her “did not have the specialized insight, knowledge or expertise to properly diagnose Nonjabulo’s illness”.

This, however, is not an isolated case.

DEVI LINK: In the past five years, the Gauteng Department of Health have been ordered by court to pay out R544 million in negligence claims.

This R544 million payout stems from 168 cases of negligence lost by the Department at the High Court and only eight cases settled out of court.
The most cases emanate from Chris Hani Baragwanath and Tembisa Hospitals.
And currently, the Department faces a staggering 10,1 billion rand in medical negligence claims.

Dr Y: It’s a function of an overburdened, overwhelmed system.

Dr Y is a senior physician at Charlotte Maxeke Hospital in Johannesburg, and says given the patient-load state doctors have to process, the number of cases against the department is no surprise.

Dr Y: On an average day a doctor can see anywhere between 20 and 60 patients.

And that says Dr. X - a senior specialist at Helen Joseph Hospital in Johannesburg – opens up a margin for error.

DR. X: You admit into hospital 40 to 50 patients. That, for example, leaves you in many cases with five to ten minutes per patient. In many cases it requires you to do everything in those 5 to 10 minutes, including putting up a drip, start antibiotics, write all the various protocols.

Compounding the risk of error for doctors on the ground is working under pressure and often without the necessary tools.

DR.Y: Often we’ll need scans to see if the patient has meningitis - if we’re able to do a lumbar puncture to diagnose it, the scans are delayed…. sometimes we’re not able to get them overnight and the next day the patient is dead and nobody knows why.

The R544 million paid out over the last 5 years could have instead bought the Gauteng Department of Health:

16 MRI scanners;
272 Anaesthetic machines; and
60 CT scanners

MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: FIRST PART OF MEDIOCRITY UPSOUND

Gauteng Health MEC, Qedani Mahlangu, who first held this position from 2009 to 2010, has been monitoring the heartbeat of her department for the past 16 months. She’s inherited a department in financial disarray and under administration that was only lifted in May. She faces deteriorating, poorly managed hospitals plagued by drug shortages or stockouts, broken equipment, and escalating negligence claims. But the MEC is adamant she will clean up the mess.

MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: will fire people etc…the attitude of our staff is a big issue…..

Despite the MEC’s stance, though the Judge found the attending doctor to be negligent in Nonjabulo’s case, the department didn’t fire or discipline the doctor as they “did not establish negligence in preparation of the case”.

And doctors on the ground say they don’t necessarily see these changes made by the MEC.


Dr X: The bad doctors know that they don’t have to bring their own standards up at all, they don’t have to work any harder and they don’t have to follow the correct procedure, because there’s very little chance of repercussion.

DEVI: Do you make surprise visits?

MEC: Yes, of course

DEVI:

MEC: and I love those, because you get the true sense of what is going on.

But Dr Y says these “surprise visits” are perhaps anticipated.

Dr Y: We’ll have visits - it’s the biggest joke in the hospital amongst the doctors, because the wards will suddenly be spick and span, there will be water jugs next to each bed and each bed will have sheets on it suddenly, with no patients in these beds. So we all know when they’re about to visit.

It’s the patients and their families, who find themselves at the mercy of a flailing health care system. They pay the ultimate price.

CELINA: She asked me didn’t they explain to you what happened to your daughter? I said: “No,
I was very shocked because I know that my daughter didn’t have any problem on her legs but now they are going to be removed.

No doctor felt it necessary to explain to Celina Kometsi why her two and a half year old daughter Thembisa’s legs would have to be amputated in 2009. The little girl went into the Far East Rand Hospital days earlier with burn wounds on her hands and arms. As Thembisa’s condition deteriorated, Celina’s cries for help fell on deaf ears.

CELINA KOMETSI: I reported you better discharge my daughter because now instead of helping her she is getting more and more pains on the body and I brought her here only with burns. I reported again she vomited, you didn’t help, now she got diarrhea, you didn’t help. Now she is weak, she can’t talk, she can’t walk. I said to the doctor: “The legs have changed, they are darker. I don’t know what is happening.”

To Celina’s horror it was discovered that her dehydrated daughter had suffered from poor blood flow - gangrene had set in in both legs.

Thembisa’s legs were amputated in October 2009. She began walking with prosthetic legs when she was four.


THEMBISA KOMETSI: I cannot jump, play other sports, but it’s alright, because I knowwho I am.

DEVI: Who are you?

THEMBISA: I am Thembisa.

DEVI: And you legs do they get sore and tired sometimes?

THEMBISA: Yes, sometimes but me when they get tired I know I must take out them to maybe and sit down and take it out and then sit and put it again.

DEVI: Can you take it out for me and show me how you do that? And your sister helps you?

THEMBISA: Yes.

THEMBISA: To be like this.

In 2010, Celina also sued the Health department and three years later Thembisa was awarded R22,1 million.

The MEC admits the department shouldn’t have defended this case.

MEC QMANHLAGU: cases like this y to argue – your child went in with two legs – meet with the family – I don’t… It is incorrect for us to defend matters that is not defensible, we have know we have wronged you, all the courts – justice dept have now – we are very resolute….indefensible.

Despite the court’s findings, the Department is still investigating liability in Thembisa’s case and have a review underway “to determine where to apportion negligence and whether to hold the doctor or system accountable”.

Medical malpractice attorney Gary Austin specializes in birth and brain injury cases. He defended Nonjabulo and says he’s seen the department defend every case he’s brought against them and feels it’s a trend.

Gary: it would be negligent of them to not do the investigation and to simply pay out, but what I find is that they defend each and every case no matter how bad the merits are.

Dr X: I am asked by the hospital to have a look at some of the cases where someone else at the hospital was being sued and to give them advice – but more often than not these cases are completely indefensible.

DEVI LINK APPLY FOR LEAVE TO APPEAL: But once the Department loses, it doesn’t end there. We have been told that in many cases they would apply for leave to appeal, and if they don’t get that, they would go straight to the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein.

And this is what happened in Nonjabulo’s case. It took four and a half years to conclude and the money was only recently paid out. MEC Mahlangu says this system will soon change.

MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: It is unjustifiable for continue to defend cases that are indefensible.

Gary and other attorneys we’ve spoken to say the department also uses delaying tactics in paying out the money.

GARY AUSTIN: Even when a court order is made for them to pay, in the majority of cases they have not paid until we have gone to their offices and had the sherif attach assets and its only once assets are attached that they then make payment.

But MEC Mahlangu denies this.

MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: We have never delayed any payment, we have always spoken to treasury.

The MEC says adding to the crippling legal and claim costs facing the department, is their discovery of syndicates alleged to be profiting from it all.

MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: There is a collusions and the trends …..
what are we doing about it? The mediators, following through the cases, lawyers who claim for people who have died who are still alive – all I am saying is there are problems, I am admitting that – but we have to admit that there are problems and we are putting systems in place to set that straight.

While the MEC works to correct these significant challenges, little can numb the pain of those whose lives have been changed forever.

CELINA: There were always tears on my eyes everyday looking at my daughter crying everyday on the pain, crying everyday but they didn’t feel shame.

DEVI: You must have had dreams for your child, what were your dreams for her?

BRENDA: I wanted Nonjabolo to be a doctor.

Dr Y: Our health department is so unwell… at the moment… that our patients are dying… they are dying the most inhumane horrible deaths.

MEC MACHLANGU: In health, we can’t make those kind of mistakes – there is no second chance, you must do it right the first time. There is only one priority – the patient who walks into the hospital must be treated with respect and dignity in a clean environment.



DEVI: When you say bad, how bad can it get?

Dr X: Its bad medical standards, so its people who have done some of the worst imaginable things, like for example taking out the wrong Kidney and cutting off wrong parts of the human body to he doesn’t know how to treat a basic pneumonia or basic diabetic emergency and these sort of things cost lives are often not visible.

Updated 01 November 2015 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 15 January 2016 Press Release: Haemorrhaging Gauteng Health Seven-year-old Nonjabulo Mavimbela was left brain-damaged and cerebral palsied after a misdiagnosis of TB-meningitis when she was almost two years old. After years of drawn-out litigation she was awarded R13.1- million. Over the past five years, taxpayers have forked out a total of R544-million in damages to compensate many victims of medical negligence like Nonjabulo. With current claims against the Gauteng Health Department at R10-billion, Carte Blanche investigates a health system seemingly failing its patients. Script: GAUTENG HEALTH SCRIPT PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK BRENDA MAVIMBELA: When I took Nonjabulo to hospital, she was a normal child, but when we came back home she is brain damaged, and there is no turning back. Seven-year old Nonjabulo Mavimbela cannot sit by herself, walk, talk or see. She is also brain damaged, has cerebral palsy and epilepsy. Her mother, Brenda and father, Lucky have to care for her 24 hours a day and both had to quit their jobs five years ago in order to do so. In 2010, Brenda and Lucky’s dreams for their daughter were shattered when she was misdiagnosed at the Far East Rand Hospital, in Johannesburg. BRENDA: She said mommy its sore here, I said: Let’s take her to the nearest hospital. They said they are going to check if there is the meningitis, they are going to do some fluid on the, a lumbar puncture. The doctor on duty diagnosed Nonjabulo with Bacterial Meningitis, when in fact she had stage 2 TB Meningitis – which untreated, progressed to stage 3, with a poor prognosis for recovery. And this misdiagnosis changed Nonjabulo’s life forever. BRENDA MAVIMBELA: I was crying, I so sad, very sad because he is telling me the way she is not going to be the same as she was before. Brenda and Lucky sued the department for negligence. Ruling in their favour and awarding Nonjabulo R13, 1 million, the Judge said that the doctor who treated her “did not have the specialized insight, knowledge or expertise to properly diagnose Nonjabulo’s illness”. This, however, is not an isolated case. DEVI LINK: In the past five years, the Gauteng Department of Health have been ordered by court to pay out R544 million in negligence claims. This R544 million payout stems from 168 cases of negligence lost by the Department at the High Court and only eight cases settled out of court. The most cases emanate from Chris Hani Baragwanath and Tembisa Hospitals. And currently, the Department faces a staggering 10,1 billion rand in medical negligence claims. Dr Y: It’s a function of an overburdened, overwhelmed system. Dr Y is a senior physician at Charlotte Maxeke Hospital in Johannesburg, and says given the patient-load state doctors have to process, the number of cases against the department is no surprise. Dr Y: On an average day a doctor can see anywhere between 20 and 60 patients. And that says Dr. X - a senior specialist at Helen Joseph Hospital in Johannesburg – opens up a margin for error. DR. X: You admit into hospital 40 to 50 patients. That, for example, leaves you in many cases with five to ten minutes per patient. In many cases it requires you to do everything in those 5 to 10 minutes, including putting up a drip, start antibiotics, write all the various protocols. Compounding the risk of error for doctors on the ground is working under pressure and often without the necessary tools. DR.Y: Often we’ll need scans to see if the patient has meningitis - if we’re able to do a lumbar puncture to diagnose it, the scans are delayed…. sometimes we’re not able to get them overnight and the next day the patient is dead and nobody knows why. The R544 million paid out over the last 5 years could have instead bought the Gauteng Department of Health: 16 MRI scanners; 272 Anaesthetic machines; and 60 CT scanners MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: FIRST PART OF MEDIOCRITY UPSOUND Gauteng Health MEC, Qedani Mahlangu, who first held this position from 2009 to 2010, has been monitoring the heartbeat of her department for the past 16 months. She’s inherited a department in financial disarray and under administration that was only lifted in May. She faces deteriorating, poorly managed hospitals plagued by drug shortages or stockouts, broken equipment, and escalating negligence claims. But the MEC is adamant she will clean up the mess. MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: will fire people etc…the attitude of our staff is a big issue….. Despite the MEC’s stance, though the Judge found the attending doctor to be negligent in Nonjabulo’s case, the department didn’t fire or discipline the doctor as they “did not establish negligence in preparation of the case”. And doctors on the ground say they don’t necessarily see these changes made by the MEC. Dr X: The bad doctors know that they don’t have to bring their own standards up at all, they don’t have to work any harder and they don’t have to follow the correct procedure, because there’s very little chance of repercussion. DEVI: Do you make surprise visits? MEC: Yes, of course DEVI: MEC: and I love those, because you get the true sense of what is going on. But Dr Y says these “surprise visits” are perhaps anticipated. Dr Y: We’ll have visits - it’s the biggest joke in the hospital amongst the doctors, because the wards will suddenly be spick and span, there will be water jugs next to each bed and each bed will have sheets on it suddenly, with no patients in these beds. So we all know when they’re about to visit. It’s the patients and their families, who find themselves at the mercy of a flailing health care system. They pay the ultimate price. CELINA: She asked me didn’t they explain to you what happened to your daughter? I said: “No, I was very shocked because I know that my daughter didn’t have any problem on her legs but now they are going to be removed. No doctor felt it necessary to explain to Celina Kometsi why her two and a half year old daughter Thembisa’s legs would have to be amputated in 2009. The little girl went into the Far East Rand Hospital days earlier with burn wounds on her hands and arms. As Thembisa’s condition deteriorated, Celina’s cries for help fell on deaf ears. CELINA KOMETSI: I reported you better discharge my daughter because now instead of helping her she is getting more and more pains on the body and I brought her here only with burns. I reported again she vomited, you didn’t help, now she got diarrhea, you didn’t help. Now she is weak, she can’t talk, she can’t walk. I said to the doctor: “The legs have changed, they are darker. I don’t know what is happening.” To Celina’s horror it was discovered that her dehydrated daughter had suffered from poor blood flow - gangrene had set in in both legs. Thembisa’s legs were amputated in October 2009. She began walking with prosthetic legs when she was four. THEMBISA KOMETSI: I cannot jump, play other sports, but it’s alright, because I knowwho I am. DEVI: Who are you? THEMBISA: I am Thembisa. DEVI: And you legs do they get sore and tired sometimes? THEMBISA: Yes, sometimes but me when they get tired I know I must take out them to maybe and sit down and take it out and then sit and put it again. DEVI: Can you take it out for me and show me how you do that? And your sister helps you? THEMBISA: Yes. THEMBISA: To be like this. In 2010, Celina also sued the Health department and three years later Thembisa was awarded R22,1 million. The MEC admits the department shouldn’t have defended this case. MEC QMANHLAGU: cases like this y to argue – your child went in with two legs – meet with the family – I don’t… It is incorrect for us to defend matters that is not defensible, we have know we have wronged you, all the courts – justice dept have now – we are very resolute….indefensible. Despite the court’s findings, the Department is still investigating liability in Thembisa’s case and have a review underway “to determine where to apportion negligence and whether to hold the doctor or system accountable”. Medical malpractice attorney Gary Austin specializes in birth and brain injury cases. He defended Nonjabulo and says he’s seen the department defend every case he’s brought against them and feels it’s a trend. Gary: it would be negligent of them to not do the investigation and to simply pay out, but what I find is that they defend each and every case no matter how bad the merits are. Dr X: I am asked by the hospital to have a look at some of the cases where someone else at the hospital was being sued and to give them advice – but more often than not these cases are completely indefensible. DEVI LINK APPLY FOR LEAVE TO APPEAL: But once the Department loses, it doesn’t end there. We have been told that in many cases they would apply for leave to appeal, and if they don’t get that, they would go straight to the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein. And this is what happened in Nonjabulo’s case. It took four and a half years to conclude and the money was only recently paid out. MEC Mahlangu says this system will soon change. MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: It is unjustifiable for continue to defend cases that are indefensible. Gary and other attorneys we’ve spoken to say the department also uses delaying tactics in paying out the money. GARY AUSTIN: Even when a court order is made for them to pay, in the majority of cases they have not paid until we have gone to their offices and had the sherif attach assets and its only once assets are attached that they then make payment. But MEC Mahlangu denies this. MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: We have never delayed any payment, we have always spoken to treasury. The MEC says adding to the crippling legal and claim costs facing the department, is their discovery of syndicates alleged to be profiting from it all. MEC QEDANI MAHLANGU: There is a collusions and the trends ….. what are we doing about it? The mediators, following through the cases, lawyers who claim for people who have died who are still alive – all I am saying is there are problems, I am admitting that – but we have to admit that there are problems and we are putting systems in place to set that straight. While the MEC works to correct these significant challenges, little can numb the pain of those whose lives have been changed forever. CELINA: There were always tears on my eyes everyday looking at my daughter crying everyday on the pain, crying everyday but they didn’t feel shame. DEVI: You must have had dreams for your child, what were your dreams for her? BRENDA: I wanted Nonjabolo to be a doctor. Dr Y: Our health department is so unwell… at the moment… that our patients are dying… they are dying the most inhumane horrible deaths. MEC MACHLANGU: In health, we can’t make those kind of mistakes – there is no second chance, you must do it right the first time. There is only one priority – the patient who walks into the hospital must be treated with respect and dignity in a clean environment. DEVI: When you say bad, how bad can it get? Dr X: Its bad medical standards, so its people who have done some of the worst imaginable things, like for example taking out the wrong Kidney and cutting off wrong parts of the human body to he doesn’t know how to treat a basic pneumonia or basic diabetic emergency and these sort of things cost lives are often not visible.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With not a single lawsuit decided in the favour of the Gauteng Health Department over the past five years, the Gauteng Health department doesn't seem in a healthy state by the way it is haemorrhaging
metadata.Summary: With not a single lawsuit decided in the favour of the Gauteng Health Department over the past five years, the Gauteng Health department doesn't seem in a healthy state by the way it is haemorrhaging money. Gauteng Health MEC recently admitted that her department had paid R544 million since 2010 for medical negligence claims. THe department had lost 168 cases and had settled eight out of court.
metadata.Further information: It seems that the department has a policy of wanting to defend every single case against them. If they lose, they apply for leave to appeal, even when leave to appeal by the residing judges are often not granted. Many of the cases makes for harrowing reading and point to negligence of a shocking nature by doctors and nurses who were on duty and treated these patients at the time. Even though these families may win these cases in court and may in the end be compensated in money, their lives are forever changed. In the legislature in September, the MEC said that the department will not fight unneccesssary court cases and will admit guilt where indicated, but this has not always been the case. Like in the case of our one case study - seven-year old Nonjabulo Mavimbela who was left brain-damaged and now has cerebral palsy after a misdiagnosis of meningitis when she was almost two years old. The department fought fruitlessly for two years to overturn the finding of negligence and her pay-out of R13,1 million. Chris Hani Baragwanath and Tembisa Hospitals in Gauteng account for the bulk of negligence cases in the province. According to the department's latest annual report, which was tabled at the Gauteng Legislature in September, legal claims against the department has risen between April 2014 and March 2015 with R4billion, now amounting to R13,1 billion - this comprises of medico-legal claims of R10,1 billion, civil claims of R1,5billion and claims of "premature termination of contracts at R1,5 billion". It is not likely that the medico-legal claims against the department would all amount into court cases and pay-outs, but it is of concern that there has been such a jump in the number. On average, the department has been paying about R200 million every year for medical negligence in terms of court settlements. The Gauteng province is not fairing the worst, but it is worrying that the department is defending every single case and also applying for leave to appeal in every single case they have lost - wasting millions of rands in litigations - money that could have been spent otherwise on proper health care development - something the province and the country are lacking. Our insiders will tell us that in Gauteng's state hospitals patient load is just too big - and maybe that is where some of the negligence in some cases originates from. Some doctors at Baragwanath Hospital have to see between 60 and 80 patients a day - nearly impossible and then to be able to give primal and basic care and attention to every patient is just not likely. There are regular drug stock-outs in the province's hospitals and in March this year, the Gauteng Health department has been labelled the worst-paying department in the province in terms of its 30-day agreement with suppliers. It seems that the problem has since been rectified, but the Gauteng Health Department is one that is bugged by poor financial management. It hasn't been able to secure a clean audit for many financial years, despite many quick turn-around strategies.
